newsitem.title: UK: UK still keen to get equal access to TARGET.
newsitem.headline: UK still keen to get equal access to TARGET.

text.p: Britain on Friday cautiously welcomed a report by the forerunner of the future European central bank on the conduct of monetary policy after the introduction of a single European currency.

But bankers made clear they would continue their fight to ensure Britain was not put at a disadvantage by being denied equal access to the new cross-border bank settlement system if it decided not to join a single currency.
The Bank of England said it welcomed "the substance" of a report by the Frankfurt-based European Monetary Institute and in particular its conclusions on monetary strategy.
"The Bank also welcomes the main elements of the framework to implement the strategy," it said.

The central bank was guarded in its comments on what for Britain are key areas of disagreement -- the introduction of minimum reserve requirements for banks and access to the future settlement system for the euro for countries which remain outside monetary union.
It said reserve requirements would be particularly damaging, amounting to a tax on business.

On access to TARGET -- the Trans-European Automated Real-Time Gross Settlement Express Transfer system -- it merely noted that "there remains an unresolved debate" and that its views had already been made known.
Germany is unhappy about allowing countries outside monetary union full access to intraday euro liquidity, fearing this will disrupt efforts to control European monetary policy.

European central bank sources have suggested that possible restrictions on "outs" could include limits on the size of intraday positions held by banks outside monetary union, or setting an earlier time for these banks to close out positions.
The EMI report saidcentral banks of countries outside the single currency would not be able to extend overnight credit in euro to institutions in their countries, adding:
"The options for national central banks outside the euro to grant intraday credit in euro to TARGET participants are still under discussion.
"Mechanisms are being prepared to prevent intraday credit, if granted to non-euro area national central banks, from spilling over into overnight credit."
The Bank of England says all EU nations should have equal access to intraday credit and does not see this as an obstacle to the smooth conduct of monetary policy.

"It is perfectly possible to prevent any tangible spillover from the settlement system into money supply creation by imposing penalties on overnight borrowing," deputy governor Howard Davies said last October.

A spokesman for the British Bankers' Association (BBA) said on Friday it still took the view that there was no tenable economic case for distinguishing between "ins" and "outs" as far as access to intraday liquidity is concerned.
"The majority of the detail appears to be sound," the spokesman said in an initial reaction to Friday's report.

"As the advocate for banks in the UK who hold more than 25 percent of greater Europe's banked deposits, the BBA will continue to press for a clear commitment to full and equal access to TARGET for "outs' as for "ins.' If that access is denied then other options are available."
Bank of England Governor Eddie George said last month that Britain was working on an alternative payments system in case it is denied equal access to TARGET, but he hoped it would not be needed.
Banking sources say the alternative could involve developing London as an offshore centre for parallel trading in euro.
City institutions fear London could lose business to Frankfurt and other financial centres if banks here are denied equal access to TARGET.
The Bank of England view is that London would not be undermined as a financial centre if Britain exercised its opt-out and decided not to join a single currency.
